name: North Face

ways.name: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
ways.season: Late July through September for the approach; the face itself favours a firm, cold night
ways.notes:
The walk-in is the standard route's: Trail #768 six and a half miles to the camp at about 2,440 ft, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, a ford to the south side near 3,700 ft, the old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber, a pass near 5,900 ft, a lake at about 5,338 ft, and a high camp on the ridge above between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft.

From camp the difference begins: continue over the col between the two glaciers at about 8,500 ft and descend onto the larger northern icefield, then traverse beneath the peak's north side to reach the foot of the face.

ways.name: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
ways.season: Midsummer through early autumn, and only as part of a larger traverse of the range
ways.notes: The first ascent came at the face from the other direction, from the col to the west, traversing the northern icefield across to the peak. That is the natural line for a party already high in this range on a multi-peak traverse rather than for a party walking in for this route alone; it involves no new trailhead but a great deal more glacier travel, and it should be planned as one leg of a bigger trip.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph describes the standard Downey/Bachelor walk-in to the ridge camp and over the col (v0) and mentions the FA line from the west only as history; v1 is for traverse parties.

name: Southwest Route

ways.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
ways.season: Late July through September, once the overgrown section is passable and the creek has dropped
ways.notes:
From the trailhead at about 1,450 ft on the river road, Trail #768 runs six and a half miles - easy, well graded, mostly flat forest walking with a suspension bridge crossing - to a camp at about 2,440 ft. The maintained trail ends there.

Continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first and fording to the south side around 3,700 ft; treat that as a real crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large old avalanche-debris zone, and this stretch is slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber even in good conditions. Above the debris the path climbs to a pass near 5,900 ft, then drops about five hundred feet to a lake at about 5,338 ft. Most parties push on from there onto the ridge above at roughly 6,400 to 6,900 ft for high camp.

ways.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
ways.season: Same window; the ridge camp is exposed to weather in a way the lake is not
ways.notes:
The lake at about 5,338 ft is reached by dropping five hundred feet off the pass and has reliable water and good camping. The ridge above it, between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft, is the higher camp most parties use, with open views across to the peaks and a much shorter summit day. The trade is exposure and a further climb at the end of an already long day in.

The drop from the pass into the lake basin holds snow into midsummer, and on snow it is normally the crux navigation of the approach day.

priorPrimaryResearch: Only one approach (Downey/Bachelor Creek); variant 1 is a camp choice, not a way in.

name: Slippery Slab Tower NE Face

ways.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
ways.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
ways.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,800 ft.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.

ways.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
ways.season: July through September
ways.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph gives both trailheads; v0 Tunnel Creek to Hope Lake then PCT south to Trap Pass is the commonly described approach with less climbing and easier tread. Not independently verified on the web.

name: Corkscrew Route

ways.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
ways.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
ways.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
ways.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.

priorPrimaryResearch: Mountaineers trip reports overwhelmingly use Bedal Creek and recommend it (avoids the North Fork Sauk fords and overgrown Cougar Creek path); the prose calls Cougar Creek 'standard' and Bedal 'often-preferred', and describes Cougar Creek in detail.

name: Neve Glacier / Standard Route

ways.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
ways.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
ways.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.

ways.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
ways.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
ways.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.

priorPrimaryResearch: Pyramid Lake/Colonial moraine camp is the standard; variant 1 is only a higher camp.

name: Standard Route / Snowking Glacier

ways.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
ways.season: June through September
ways.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.

ways.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
ways.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
ways.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.

priorPrimaryResearch: The Kindy Creek roadbed and Kindy Ridge is the only approach. Variant 1 is only a choice of camp.

name: South Arete

ways.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.

ways.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
ways.season: Highway opening through Jun
ways.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.

priorPrimaryResearch: Variant 1 is the same Blue Lake line under early-season snow; prose describes the summer climbers' path.

name: Direct East Buttress

ways.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the right, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.

ways.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
ways.season: Highway opening through Jun
ways.notes: Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph describes the Spire Gully approach from the hairpin (v0), with early-season snow noted in passing; v1 is the same line with snow. Seasons already differ.

name: South Face

ways.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
ways.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
ways.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.

ways.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
ways.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
ways.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.

ways.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
ways.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

priorPrimaryResearch: Andrews Creek is the common/quickest approach (Country Highpoints, SummitPost); Cathedral Driveway is a longer drive and a climb-out finish.

name: South Gully/South Spur

ways.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
ways.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
ways.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.

ways.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
ways.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
ways.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.

priorPrimaryResearch: Guye Peak's South Gully is known as a winter snow climb approached from Summit West through Commonwealth, and variant 1 says the summer version is 'not well loved'. The paragraph describes the Alpental/south-side summer access, which is variant 1.

name: South Spur

ways.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 16 miles in, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.

ways.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
ways.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
ways.notes:
An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. The river is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.

priorPrimaryResearch: The paragraph calls Easy Ridge over the Impasse to Perfect Pass 'the standard approach', and variant 1 is presented as the alternative.

name: West Ridge (Beckey Route)

ways.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
ways.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
ways.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.

ways.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
ways.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
ways.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.

priorPrimaryResearch: Only one approach (Depot Creek); variant 1 is a camp choice. Prose describes Depot Creek.
